subsystems.name: Key encapsulation (ML-KEM)
subsystems.role: replaces RSA and Diffie–Hellman key exchange with a lattice problem no known quantum algorithm solves.

subsystems.name: Digital signatures
subsystems.role: authenticates software, servers and documents; two families are standardised because they fail differently.

subsystems.name: Symmetric primitives and hashing
subsystems.role: bulk encryption and integrity, where quantum computers are far less threatening.

subsystems.name: Hybrid transition layer
subsystems.role: runs classical and post-quantum algorithms together so a break in either alone is not fatal.

subsystems.name: Cryptographic inventory and agility
subsystems.role: finds every place RSA or elliptic-curve crypto hides, and makes swapping it routine.

subsystems.name: Hardware and embedded implementation
subsystems.role: puts the new algorithms into chips that must resist side-channel and fault attacks.

buildSteps.title: Inventory the cryptography
buildSteps.detail: Scan code, certificates, firmware and protocols to find every use of RSA, Diffie–Hellman and elliptic curves, including inside devices that are hard to update.

buildSteps.title: Pick algorithms and parameters
buildSteps.detail: Choose from the NIST standards — ML-KEM for key exchange, ML-DSA or SLH-DSA for signatures — sized to the data's lifetime and the device's memory.

buildSteps.title: Implement defensively
buildSteps.detail: Write constant-time code that leaks nothing through timing or power draw, and test against published vectors.

buildSteps.title: Validate
buildSteps.detail: Run the algorithms through formal cryptographic validation and certification programmes before deploying them in critical systems.

buildSteps.title: Deploy in hybrid mode
buildSteps.detail: Enable classical-plus-post-quantum handshakes in browsers, messengers, SSH and VPNs so a single algorithm failing does not open the connection.

buildSteps.title: Move signatures into the chain of trust
buildSteps.detail: Reissue root and intermediate certificates, code-signing keys and firmware-signing keys with post-quantum signatures, working from the shortest-lived to the longest-lived.

buildSteps.title: Protect stored and archived data
buildSteps.detail: Re-encrypt or re-key long-lived secrets and backups, since traffic recorded today can be decrypted once a quantum computer arrives.

buildSteps.title: Retire the old algorithms
buildSteps.detail: Once the hybrid stack is proven and dependencies are gone, switch off RSA and elliptic-curve modes and keep agility so the next migration is easier.

prerequisites.why: the hardness of learning-with-errors problems underpins the new key exchange and signature schemes.
they offer a conservative fallback whose security rests only on hash functions.
FIPS 203, 204 and 205, published in August 2024, give vendors one interoperable target.

prerequisites.tech: Cryptographic agility in software and hardware
prerequisites.why: many systems hard-code one algorithm and cannot be re-keyed without replacement.
post-quantum maths uses large matrices and sampling that are harder to make leak-proof than RSA.

prerequisites.tech: Quantum computers able to run Shor's algorithm at scale
prerequisites.why: they are the threat being defended against; today's machines are far too small and error-prone.

pathway.milestone: hybrid key exchange already on by default in major browsers, messengers and OpenSSH
pathway.unlocks: protection against recorded-now-decrypt-later attacks on today's sessions.

pathway.milestone: post-quantum signatures inside certificate authorities, code signing and firmware updates
pathway.unlocks: a chain of trust that survives a quantum break.

pathway.milestone: national-security and regulated sectors complete migration ahead of long-dated deadlines
pathway.unlocks: proof that whole enterprises, not just browsers, can convert.

pathway.milestone: RSA and elliptic curves retired and agility treated as routine engineering
pathway.unlocks: resilience to whatever the next cryptanalytic surprise turns out to be.
